raw_text:
For five years my world was a circle of stone and a spiral of stairs; its boundaries were the high water mark upon the shore and the reach of the lamp’s singular beam across the churning sea. My guardian, a silent man whose face was a map of sorrows I could not read, would arrive with the new moon, leaving provisions of salt fish, flour, and oil; he would depart without a word, and I would be left again to the cries of the gulls and the ceaseless monologue of the waves. In this isolation I felt no unhappiness, for I knew no alternative to it; my life was a simple machine of duties, and I was but one of its untroubled cogs.

The night of the storm, however, rent the placid veil of my existence. I watched from the lantern room as the sea, whipped into a frenzy of black and white, devoured a small merchant ship, its lights extinguished one by one like dying stars. The next morning, when the waters had retreated with a sullen murmur, I saw that the tempest had bequeathed to me a strange and terrible gift: survivors. There were five of them, huddled on my beach, their forms scarcely distinguishable from the detritus of their vessel. I remained hidden in my tower, a fearful and silent observer of this sudden intrusion of humanity.

Their days were at first consumed with grief and the grim labour of survival. I saw them construct a crude shelter from the splintered timbers of their ship; I watched as the captain, a man of stern visage, rationed their meagre findings with a heavy hand, incurring the resentful glares of a younger, more impetuous sailor. A woman amongst them, whose name I later learned was Elodie, would often sit apart from the others, her gaze lost upon the horizon, and from her quiet weeping I began to comprehend the nature of loss, a concept heretofore as alien to me as the dark side of the moon.

While I improved in my understanding of their speech, which I caught in fragments on the wind, I also learned from a book which the tide had mercifully spared. It was a volume of philosophical treatises, and from its dense pages I gleaned the strange systems of human thought. The book spoke of reason and passion, of the social contract, of virtue and of vice. I read of the great men who had built empires of logic and of the fools who had torn them down for a moment’s fleeting pleasure; I learned of justice and law, of property, and of the thousand invisible threads which bind one person to another in a society.

These revelations inspired in me a profound disquiet. Was this the world from which I had been so completely severed? This tapestry of obligation, of love, of envy, of immense wealth and squalid poverty? The words induced me to turn towards myself. I learned that the qualities most esteemed were intellect, courage, and a place within the great family of man. A person might be praised for their mind or their deeds, but without connection to others, they were considered a phantom, an outcast doomed to wander the bleak wildernesses of the world. And what was I? Of my own past I knew nothing; I possessed no family, no fortune, no name but the one I had whispered to myself in the echoing silence of my stone room.

I was, besides, a creature of utter ignorance; I could predict the turning of the tides and the phases of the moon, but I knew nothing of a mother’s kindness or a father’s guidance. When I looked in the salt-stained glass, I saw a face made pale by solitude and eyes widened by a constant, unasked question. Was I, then, a monster of a different sort, not of body but of soul, a being defined only by absence, from whom all society fled and whom all society had disowned?

I cannot describe to you the agony which these reflections inflicted upon me; I tried to dispel them by focusing on my duties, but knowledge, once gained, would not be dismissed. Oh, that I had for ever remained in my ignorant peace, my senses filled only with the turning of the light and the roar of the sea!

Of what a strange nature is thought! It takes root in the mind like a hardy weed on a barren cliff. I wished sometimes to return to my former state of placid vacancy, but I learned that there was but one cure for the pain of consciousness, and that was a finality I feared yet could not comprehend. I admired the resilience and ingenuity of the survivors, and loved the gentle manner in which the woman, Elodie, spoke to the youngest of their party, a boy barely on the cusp of manhood. But I was shut out from all intercourse with them, a ghost in my own home, and the sounds of their life, their arguments and their laughter, served only to deepen the chasm which separated me from them. The warmth of their fire was not for me. The shared hope in the captain’s speech and the quiet comradeship of their miserable meal were not for me. Unhappy, isolated wretch! What was I? The question returned again and again, to be answered only with the groaning of the wind through the stones of my lonely prison.

learn, I was not at liberty to discover. Their conversations, however, soon revealed the unhappy truth.

The father of Safie, a man of considerable wealth and influence among his own people, had fallen under the unjust suspicion of the French government. He was seized, condemned to perpetual imprisonment, and his fortune confiscated upon the pretext of some imagined conspiracy against the state. The Turk, whose pride was as great as his misfortune, chafed under this tyranny and secretly plotted his escape, but he possessed no means by which to execute his design. It was in this state of despair that he learned of the eloquence and benevolent reputation of De Lacey’s son, Felix, who had distinguished himself at the bar by his passionate defences of the oppressed.

The Turk, whose name was never uttered by my protectors, contrived to send a message to the young advocate, promising immense riches if Felix would but aid his escape from the dungeons of Paris. Felix, however, was not a man to be moved by the lure of gold. His heart was fired by a sense of the gross injustice done to the stranger, and he burned with a desire to right this unpardonable wrong. He visited the Turk in his cell and was so moved by his narrative of suffering, and by the dignity with which he bore his chains, that he vowed to devote himself entirely to the cause of his liberation.

In the course of his visits, Felix was not always alone; he was sometimes accompanied by his sister Agatha, and upon one occasion, by the Turk’s own daughter, the Arabian Safie. She had been permitted, by a rare indulgence, to see her father before he was to be immured for ever from the light of day. I have before described to you her beauty, but words cannot convey the celestial expression of her countenance as she knelt at her father’s feet, her dark eyes swimming with tears of love and despair. From that moment, Felix was no longer the master of his own heart. He saw in Safie the embodiment of all that was gentle and lovely, a divine spirit trapped, like her father, in a web of cruelty and prejudice. He now pursued the Turk’s freedom with a twofold ardour, one part born of his noble indignation at injustice, the other of his passionate love for the beautiful Arabian.

After many weeks of perilous contrivance, during which Felix risked his own life and liberty a thousand times, a plan was at last perfected. On the very eve of the Turk’s transfer to a more secure and distant fortress, Felix succeeded in conveying to him the tools and instructions for his escape. That night, the merchant fled from Paris, accompanied by his daughter, and guided by Felix, they travelled by unfrequented roads towards the frontiers of France. They had agreed to meet at Leghorn, in Italy, where the Turk had promised Felix the hand of his daughter as a reward for his service.

Felix, his heart swelling with triumph and love, returned to Paris to settle his affairs and prepare his father and sister for their departure. But his joy was to be of short duration. The French government, enraged by the escape of its prisoner, launched a furious investigation. The part which Felix had played was soon discovered; his actions, which had sprung from the purest motives of justice and compassion, were branded as treason. In a single, terrible blow, the entire De Lacey family was ruined. The old man, blind and helpless, and the gentle Agatha, were seized as accomplices in the flight of the Turk and cast into prison. Their moderate fortune was confiscated, and they were condemned, after a mockery of a trial, to perpetual exile from their native country.

For five months they languished in a dreadful dungeon, suffering every misery that poverty and disgrace can inflict upon persons of refined sensibility. Felix, upon learning of his family’s fate, was torn by the most agonizing conflict. His duty called him back to Paris to share their imprisonment, but his love for Safie and his promise to meet her in Leghorn pulled him with equal force towards Italy. In the end, filial piety triumphed; he wrote to Safie, explaining the calamitous turn of events and releasing her from any obligation to him, before surrendering himself to the authorities.

Here the story of my friends took a turn which filled me with the utmost indignation. The treacherous Turk, upon reaching the safety of Italian soil and learning that his benefactor was now a ruined and powerless exile, forgot all his promises. The prospect of marrying his daughter to a penniless fugitive was odious to him. He had always disliked the idea of her union with a Christian, and now that Felix could be of no further use to him, he resolved to break his word. He lingered in Leghorn for a time, fearing that Felix might yet appear and demand his bride, but when news of the De Laceys’ condemnation and exile reached him, he prepared to depart for his native land, taking his unwilling daughter with him.

Safie, however, was not a creature to be so easily controlled. Her mother had been a Christian Arab, seized and enslaved by the Turks, but who, in her captivity, had instilled in her daughter the tenets of her own faith and a love of intellectual freedom utterly at variance with the servile expectations of her new countrymen. Safie loathed the thought of returning to Asia, to be immured in a harem and treated as a mere object of sensual pleasure. Her brief acquaintance with Felix had opened her eyes to a world of intellectual companionship and mutual respect between the sexes, and her heart yearned for the liberty which her lover had represented.

Discovering her father’s perfidious intentions, and finding some papers which revealed the location of the De Laceys’ humble exile in Germany, she resolved upon a bold and desperate course. With a small sum of money and her jewels, she secretly left her father’s house, accompanied by an attendant who knew the German language, and set out to find the cottage of her beloved Felix. They journeyed for many weeks, but misfortune pursued them; her attendant fell ill and died in a small town on the frontier, leaving Safie alone, ignorant of the language and with her funds nearly exhausted. Yet her courage did not fail her. She remembered the name of the town near which the De Laceys lived, and by showing the written direction to the drivers of public conveyances, she at last, after so many trials, arrived at the cottage and threw herself into the arms of her friends.

You may well imagine the joy that her arrival brought to the sorrowing exiles. She was a ray of sunshine piercing the gloom of their miserable existence. Her gay and animated spirit revived their drooping hopes, and her presence transformed their humble hovel into a place of delight. It was her appearance which I had witnessed, and which had first awakened in me the complex feelings that were now the fabric of my being.

This narrative, which I pieced together from their many conversations, affected me profoundly. It presented a picture of injustice and ingratitude on the one hand, and of heroic virtue and devoted love on the other. I sympathized with the sufferings of my protectors, and my heart burned with indignation against the treacherous Turk and the cruel government of France. But these feelings were soon eclipsed by a more personal and agonizing train of thought.

The story of the De Laceys was a story of connection, of mutual bonds, of love and sacrifice. Even in their ruin, they had each other. Felix had a father and sister who loved him; Agatha had a brother and father who cherished her; and now Safie had joined their circle, bound to them by gratitude and love. They were a society in miniature, a world of interlocking affections and duties.

But what of me? As I listened, the terrible truth of my own isolation pressed upon me with a weight that was almost physical. I had no father to be ruined by my actions, no sister to languish in a dungeon for my sake. I had no lover to cross a continent for, no beautiful Arabian to fill my hovel with light and music. I was a single, solitary atom, unconnected to the great chain of being. If I were to suffer, I would suffer alone; if I were to die, no one would weep for me or even mark my passing. The love that bound the cottagers together was the very fabric of their world, a fabric from which I was irrevocably cut.

These reflections became a torment. I would watch them through the chink in the wall, see the tender glance that passed between Felix and Safie, observe the gentle way Agatha cared for her blind father, and a feeling of envy so bitter and so profound would take possession of me that I would be forced to retreat into the darkest corner of my hovel and give vent to my misery in groans which I dared not allow to be heard. I saw the blissful state of my protectors, and I felt the hell that was growing within me. Their happiness did not gladden me; it mocked me. It was a mirror in which I saw my own monstrous solitude reflected.

The spring advanced, and with it, my education. Yet every new piece of knowledge, every new insight into the world of man, only served to increase my wretchedness. I learned of the delicate and mysterious bonds of family. I heard Felix speak of his reverence for his father, and I saw the old man’s face light up with paternal pride. I heard the women speak of the joys of motherhood, of the sacred charge of a child, and my mind, for the first time, turned to the question of my own origin.

Where was my mother? Where was my father? I had no infant recollections, no memories of gentle caresses or loving smiles. My first awareness was of a confused and painful state, of light that hurt my eyes and sensations that overwhelmed me. Had a father’s hand guided my first steps? Had a mother’s breast nourished me? I knew nothing. I was a miserable wretch, an abortion, a thing flung into the world without care or connection, to be stumbled upon and then shunned.

This question, "What was I?", which had before been a matter of philosophical curiosity, now became a cry of existential agony. I was not merely different in form; I was different in essence. I was a being without a history, without a people, without a single soul on the entire globe to whom I could claim kinship. Was I then truly a monster? Not because of my stature or my features, which I had never seen, but because of this utter, absolute solitude. This was a degradation far below that of the blind mole or the harmless worm, for they, at least, were part of a species; they had a place in the natural order of things. I had none.

My only solace was in the night. When the cottagers were asleep and the world was mine alone, I would wander in the woods and allow my sorrow to pour forth. I would look at the moon, that serene and silent orb, and address it in the impassioned language of my heart. "You," I would cry, "are my solitary companion. You see my wretchedness, and you do not flee. But you, too, are distant and unfeeling. You shine upon my misery, but you cannot alleviate it."

One night, during my accustomed ramble, my thoughts were darker than ever before. The story of Safie’s journey, of her courage and devotion, haunted me. It was a testament to the power of human connection, a power I could admire but never possess. In a state of agitation bordering on madness, I returned to my hovel and began to rummage through the few possessions I had gathered in my former wanderings. Among them was a leather portmanteau which I had found in the woods, and in it, some books and papers. In my earlier state of ignorance I had been unable to decipher them, but now, with the key of language, a new world was open to me.

With trembling hands, I lit my rude lamp, a vessel I had fashioned from a gourd and filled with animal fat, and examined my treasure. There were three books: one was a volume of Plutarch’s _Lives_, another was Goethe’s _The Sorrows of Young Werther_, and the third was Milton’s _Paradise Lost_. What a strange and potent trinity of knowledge to fall into the hands of such a wretch as I!

I read them with an avidity that was almost feverish. Plutarch taught me of the heroes of antiquity, of the grandeur of public life, and of the virtues of patriotism and self-sacrifice. He filled my mind with high and noble sentiments, but he also showed me societies from which I was utterly excluded. I could admire the lawgivers and warriors, but I could never be one of them. I was an outcast, a pariah, not a citizen.

_The Sorrows of Young Werther_ resonated more deeply with my own condition. I read of a sensitive and passionate soul, tormented by feelings he could not control, and isolated from the object of his love. I felt for Werther as for a brother, and I wept over his sorrows. But even he, in his despair, was not as alone as I. He had friends to write to; he had a past; he was a human being, and his death was a matter of consequence. I, on the other hand, was a creature of a different order. If I were to put an end to my own miserable existence, it would be as if a leaf had fallen from a tree in the midst of a vast and unpeopled forest.

But it was _Paradise Lost_ that moved me most profoundly. I read it, not as a work of fiction, but as a true history of the origins of the world. It seemed to explain my own place in the universe, or rather, my lack of one. Like Adam, I was a creature newly formed, with no apparent connection to any other being in existence. But his state was far different from mine. He came from the hands of God a perfect creature, happy and prosperous, guarded by the especial care of his Creator. He was allowed to converse with and acquire knowledge from beings of a superior nature. But I was wretched, helpless, and alone. Many times I considered myself to be the fallen angel, Satan, for I, too, had been cast out from a world of light and joy. I sympathized with his despair and his envy. Like him, when I viewed the bliss of my protectors, the bitter gall of envy rose within me. But even Satan had his companions, his fellow devils, to admire and encourage him. I was solitary and abhorred.

I was solitary and abhorred.

I, who had looked upon the delicate forms of the cottagers with a kind of holy reverence, now learned that my own flesh was a patchwork of corruption, my limbs assembled from the dismembered dead. The Turk, at first surprised, soon perceived in the earnest countenance and energetic gestures of Felix a promise of success, and he listened with gratitude. His gratitude, however, was soon mingled with a more selfish motive. He had observed the grace and beauty of his daughter, Safie, with a father’s pride, but he had also noted the profound impression she had made upon the young Frenchman. The wily merchant, therefore, to ensure the fidelity of his deliverer, promised him the hand of his daughter in marriage. Felix was too much in love to perceive the snare; he joyfully and ardently accepted the proposal.

Safie herself was a party to this engagement. Her mother, a Christian Arab, had been seized and made a slave by the Turks, but had in that degraded state captivated the heart of her master, and become his wife. Unlike the other women of her country, she had not been confined to the ignorance and seclusion of a harem. She had imbibed a spirit of independence and possessed a mind of a superior order, which she had laboured to cultivate in her daughter. Safie was taught to aspire to a higher intellectual and social station than the females of her native land could attain. The prospect of returning to Asia and being immured within the walls of a seraglio filled her with horror; she had rejoiced, therefore, when her father had announced his intention of settling in a European country. The idea of marrying a Christian and remaining in a land where women were treated as rational beings, not as mere playthings, was a vision of delight to her.

Felix, in the meantime, devoted every thought to the execution of his project. He laboured with unceasing vigilance, and at length, on the very eve of the day fixed for the Turk’s execution, he contrived to conduct him in safety from his prison. He led him and his daughter to a place of security without the city walls, and after providing them with a sum of money, he arranged for them to await him at Leghorn, in Italy, where he promised to join them. He returned to Paris, but his benevolent design was not destined to proceed without a dreadful reverse. The flight of the merchant was discovered, and the French government, enraged at the escape of their victim, seized upon old De Lacey and Agatha as accomplices in the crime. They were cast into a dungeon, and their trial, a mere mockery of justice, soon followed.

This terrible news reached Felix while he was on his way to Leghorn. Overwhelmed with grief, he hesitated for a moment, torn between his love for the Arabian and his filial duty. But he did not long deliberate; he hastened back to Paris, delivered himself into the hands of the law, and threw himself at the feet of the magistrates. His self-accusation, however, did not exonerate his family. They were all condemned; their entire fortune was confiscated, and they were sentenced to perpetual exile. They found a miserable asylum in the cottage in Germany where I now beheld them, stripped of all their possessions and living in a state of the most profound poverty and dejection.

The perfidious Turk, for whom my friends had sacrificed their all, witnessed their ruin with a callous indifference. When he learned that Felix, far from being able to transport him to Constantinople, was himself a beggar and an outcast, he forgot his promises of gratitude and the hand of his daughter. The thoughts of an alliance with a disgraced family were odious to him. He offered Felix a paltry sum of money, which the young man rejected with scorn, and soon after, the treacherous merchant departed for his native country, commanding his daughter to follow him. She knew the name of her lover’s native country, but was ignorant of the specific place of his retreat. The journey I now undertook was of a character far different from my former wanderings. Before, I had been a creature of circumstance, driven by instinct and a burgeoning curiosity; now, I was an arrow shot from the bow of my own cultivated hatred, my path fixed, my target known. The name of Geneva was a brand upon my mind, and the image of my creator, as depicted in his own accursed journal, was a spectre that walked always before me, beckoning me towards my terrible destiny.

The autumn advanced, and the leaves, which had before sheltered me, now fell in showers, leaving the branches bare and exposing my form to the casual glance of any who might pass. My route lay to the south and west, and I was forced to exercise the utmost caution, for I now understood with perfect clarity the reception I might expect from mankind. I travelled only by night, when the world was asleep, and hid myself during the day in the thickest woods, in caves, or in deserted outhouses. My prodigious strength, which I had once regarded with a kind of innocent wonder, now became my greatest asset; I could traverse difficult terrain with a speed no human could match and leap over obstacles which would have halted any other pursuer. My sustenance was the same as it had ever been, berries, nuts, and roots, but I now took them without any feeling of communion with the earth, which had become to me but a stage for my misery.

Often, as I lay concealed in some dark recess, I would draw forth the papers from my pocket. I would read again and again the account of my creation, the words of disgust, the flight of my maker. Each reading was like pouring fresh poison into a festering wound; it fed my rage and solidified my purpose, extinguishing any nascent spark of doubt or pity. How could I pity him who had no pity for me? He had endowed me with life, with perceptions, with desires, and then, horrified by his own handiwork, had cast me aside as a thing of filth. I learned from his journal of his family, of a father he revered, a friend named Clerval he cherished, and a cousin, an adopted sister, Elizabeth, whom he adored with a celestial love. These names, these relationships, became to me symbols of all I was denied. They were the warm hearth from which I was eternally cast out into the cold. And a new, dark thought began to take root in the fertile soil of my despair: if I could not share in his happiness, I could, at the very least, ensure he shared in my misery. Vengeance required more than a simple confrontation; it demanded a deep and abiding sorrow, a reflection of my own.

Winter came, and with it, a new trial of my endurance. The earth was covered in a sheet of brilliant, unforgiving white. The cold was intense, and the winds that howled through the leafless forests seemed to carry upon them the wails of all the world’s forsaken souls. Yet my frame, hardier than a man’s, resisted the frost. The very elements that would have killed a human being were to me but another hardship to be overcome. I crossed frozen rivers and scaled mountains of ice, my feet sure where a man’s would have slipped to his doom. Sometimes, from a high crag, I would look down upon the villages nestled in the valleys, their windows glowing with a warm, yellow light. I saw the smoke curling from their chimneys and imagined the families gathered within, sharing stories and laughter, secure in their mutual affection. The sight would fill me with a bitter, inconsolable anguish. It was a tableau of a life I could never know, a heaven from which I was irrevocably barred. My heart, which had once swelled with love for the cottagers, was now a knot of ice and fire, and I would turn from the sight with a groan of despair and a renewed oath of vengeance against him who had made me to be this solitary fiend.

My progress was slow, for the nights were dark and the ground was often treacherous. But spring returned at last. The sun regained its strength, the snows melted, and the rivers, swollen with the thaw, rushed through the valleys. A strange and unwelcome softening occurred in my own breast. I saw the little flowers bursting from the earth, I heard the birds singing in the budding trees, and my heart, against its will, was moved. The feelings of hope and benevolence, which I had believed utterly extinguished, flickered weakly within me. For a few days, I forgot my purpose and allowed myself to feel a part of the rejuvenation of nature. This brief respite, this momentary lapse in my guard, was to be the preface to my final and most absolute condemnation.

One day, as I wandered near the banks of a rapid stream, my senses were arrested by the sight of a young girl, a child of perhaps five or six years, playing amongst the trees. Her laughter was like the music of the birds, and her innocent beauty was a balm to my tormented soul. I concealed myself behind a thicket, content to observe her, my heart filled with a gentle, painful adoration. Suddenly, her foot slipped on the damp bank, and with a cry of terror, she fell into the swift current. Without a moment’s hesitation, my long-suppressed instincts of compassion and goodness took command. I rushed from my hiding place and plunged into the icy water. The torrent was strong, but my power was greater; I seized the child, who was already being carried away, and with a few powerful strokes, brought her safely to the shore.

I laid her gently on the grass, where she lay insensible. I was chafing her hands and attempting to restore her when I heard a shout. A man, who I presumed to be a rustic and perhaps the child’s father, came running towards me. Upon seeing me bending over the girl, his face contorted not with gratitude, but with horror and fury. I saw lights in the windows, and I imagined the scene of domestic bliss within. I pictured him, my creator, surrounded by a loving family, his features composed in that gentle benevolence which I had seen him bestow upon his chemical apparatus, but never upon me, his living, breathing progeny. The sight of the happy family group, which I sometimes glimpsed as a servant opened a door or a curtain was momentarily drawn aside, did not soften my heart, as the sight of the cottagers had once done; it inflamed my hatred and lent a keener edge to my desire for revenge. The world had judged me a demon; I would therefore play the part, and my first act would be upon the stage of his own happiness.

I did not, however, act with precipitation. My intellect, sharpened by solitude and suffering, guided my fury. I knew that to reveal myself to him at once would be to grant him a swift conclusion, while my design was far more intricate. He must be made to feel my power before he saw my face. He must learn that the monster he had cast out possessed the ability to reach into the very heart of his sanctuary and pluck out its choicest treasures. I lurked for several days in the woods of Plainpalais, through which I knew the family must often pass on their excursions. I subsisted on berries and the unfortunate creatures of the forest, my thoughts a constant, feverish meditation on the nature of the blow I should first inflict.

Chance, or perhaps a more malignant destiny, soon presented me with the instrument of my design. It was on an evening of serene beauty, when the last rays of the setting sun gilded the snowy summit of Mont Blanc, that I saw a child of angelic beauty wander from his companions and enter the wood where I was concealed. He was a lovely boy, with curling hair, and a countenance of such perfect innocence that it seemed to mock the twisted and abhorrent ruin of my own. A sudden, foolish impulse seized me, a faint echo of that yearning for companionship which had once defined my existence. Perhaps, I thought, this creature, so young and uncorrupted by the prejudices of the world, would not flee from me in terror. His mind was a blank page, not yet scribbled over with the hateful doctrines of society. I might seize him, carry him to a hidden cave, and raise him to be my companion and my friend. He would not behold my deformity with the same eyes as his elders; he would learn to love me for the devotion I would lavish upon him.

Filled with this mad and desperate hope, I emerged from my hiding place and stood before him. My intention was to speak gently, to soothe his fears with the soft accents I had learned from my beloved cottagers. But the moment his eyes fell upon my form, his angelic features were contorted into a mask of terror and disgust. He placed his hands before his eyes and uttered a shrill scream that pierced my ears like a hot needle. “Let me go,” he cried, as I reached out my hand towards him; “monster! Ugly wretch! You wish to eat me and tear me to pieces. You are an ogre. Let me go, or I will tell my papa.”

“Boy,” I said, my voice trembling with an emotion that was no longer gentle, “you must come with me. Do not be afraid; I will not harm you.”

He struggled violently in my grasp. “Hideous monster!” he shrieked. “My papa is a syndic; he is M. Frankenstein. He will punish you. You dare not keep me.”

Frankenstein! The name was a thunderclap that shattered the last vestiges of my fleeting compassion. This child, this beautiful, innocent creature, was his. This was the flesh of my creator, the beloved progeny for whom he had abandoned his own monstrous creation. The irony was so bitter, so profound, that it choked me. Here, then, was the instrument of my first lesson to Frankenstein; here was a vessel into which I could pour a measure of my own despair and send it back to its source. A paroxysm of fury, black and absolute, seized my soul. I saw not a child, but an effigy of my tormentor, a symbol of all the joy, the love, and the acceptance that had been denied me. My fingers, as if possessed of a will of their own, closed around his delicate throat. He struggled for a moment, his eyes wide with a terror that I now relished, and then he was still.

I gazed upon the lifeless form at my feet, and a feeling of grim and terrible satisfaction filled me. The deed was done. I had struck my first blow. I had proven that I was not merely a passive recipient of suffering, but an active agent of it. I felt a surge of power, a dizzying sense of my own capacity to inflict misery, which was a horrid substitute for the happiness I craved. In that moment, I exulted in my own damnation. I was a monster, and I had at last committed a monstrous act.

As I stood over the body, my eye was caught by a glittering object on his breast. It was a locket, which I seized and opened. It contained a miniature portrait of a woman of exquisite beauty. I knew instinctively that this must be the boy’s mother, my creator’s own lamented parent, a face radiant with a tenderness he never knew how to bestow on me. I gazed at the portrait for a long time. She was beautiful, but her beauty was a torment to me. It was the beauty of a world from which I was forever cast out. I detested the serene and lovely face that smiled at me, a smile that seemed to proclaim a happiness rooted in family and affection, the very things my existence rendered impossible. I almost determined to tear the portrait to pieces, but a more subtle and more devilish idea entered my mind.

Revenge, I thought, ought not to be so simple as a single death. The sorrow of this child’s absence must be compounded by another, more intricate form of suffering. It must be entwined with injustice, the very poison that had corrupted my own soul. I would not merely take a life; I would corrupt a reputation. I would turn the sword of human society, with its blind judgments and its merciless laws, back upon itself. I wandered for several hours in the darkness, the locket clutched in my hand, my mind alight with its infernal purpose. My wanderings led me to a barn, not far from the spot where I had committed my crime. Seeking shelter, I entered and found a young woman asleep on a bed of straw. By the light of the moon, which streamed through a crack in the roof, I saw her face. She was lovely, with a healthy bloom on her cheeks and an expression of perfect innocence in her slumber. She was a picture of rustic peace and virtue. For a moment, I was moved. I saw in her the embodiment of the simple goodness I had adored in Agatha. A profound sense of my own exclusion washed over me; she could sleep, but I was doomed to perpetual wakefulness. She could dream of love and happiness, while my only dreams were of hatred and revenge.

This wave of self-pity quickly curdled into a renewed bitterness. Why should she enjoy this peace? Why should she be loved and trusted, while I, who had once been benevolent and good, was abhorred and hunted? She was one of them, one of the human race that had scorned and rejected me. She was a servant, I surmised, one of the very class doomed to suffer for the sins of the powerful, yet she appeared happy. The injustice of it all, as I perceived it, was maddening. I would make her a part of my design. I would use her to demonstrate the folly of human justice. The world had declared me a fiend; I would show them how easily their own systems could be turned to fiendish ends.

“Here is my opportunity,” I whispered to the sleeping air. “You, who appear so gentle and good, you shall bear the blame for my deed. The world will look upon you as they have looked upon me, with suspicion and hatred. Your innocence will not save you.”

With a steady hand, a hand that did not tremble, I unclasped the locket from my grasp. I knelt beside the sleeping girl. Her breathing was soft and regular. A gentle smile played upon her lips, as if she were in the midst of a pleasant dream. For an instant, I hesitated. The impulse to destroy her was at war with the lingering image of the goodness I had once revered. But the thought of my creator, of the boy’s dead body, and of my own eternal solitude, hardened my heart. This was not a crime, I told myself; it was a lesson. It was an act of war. I carefully slipped the chain of the locket into a fold of her dress, placing the miniature where it would be easily discovered. She stirred slightly in her sleep, but did not wake.

I then crept from the barn and fled into the mountains, my work for the night complete. I had not only extinguished a life dear to my enemy, but I had also planted the seeds of a second, more insidious tragedy. I had framed an innocent being for my crime, and I felt a chilling sense of intellectual pride in the cleverness of my own malice. I had learned the lessons of mankind well. I had learned that to be powerful, one must be cruel, and that to be safe, one must be willing to sacrifice the innocent. I was no longer the weeping, pleading wretch who had been spurned by the De Laceys. I was a being of calculated malevolence, an arbiter of a justice of my own making.

I hid myself amongst the highest peaks, in the icy solitudes of the glaciers, a landscape that was a fitting mirror to the coldness of my own heart. From these heights, I could look down upon the world of men, a world I now held in utter contempt. I waited, listening on the winds for news of the consequences of my actions. I soon learned that my plan had succeeded beyond my darkest hopes. The child’s body was discovered. The family was plunged into a grief so profound it seemed to shake the very foundations of their home. And then, as I had willed it, the locket was found on the person of the sleeping servant, Justine Moritz. The circumstantial evidence was overwhelming; she was accused, tried, and, despite her protestations of innocence, condemned.

I felt a perverse species of delight in hearing the details of her trial. I learned that she was bewildered, that her defence was confused, and that her own confessor had tormented her into a false admission of guilt. Society, in its blind rage, had devoured one of its own. My creator, Frankenstein, had not only lost his brother, but he had also stood by and watched as an innocent member of his own household was led to the gallows for a crime she did not commit. His suffering must have been immense, a torment of grief compounded by guilt. This was the revenge I had sought, a sorrow that was not clean and sharp like the blade of a knife, but a festering wound, poisoned by injustice and remorse.

Such was the history of my first acts of vengeance. I had shed innocent blood, and I felt no remorse, only a chilling sense of justice fulfilled. My heart was hardened into a substance as unyielding as the rock on which I sat. The gentle creature who had wept at the music of the Arabian girl was dead, and in his place stood a fiend. I had declared war upon the whole of human kind, and most of all upon you, my creator. And so, having tasted the power of inflicting pain, I came to a new resolution. I would not live out my miserable existence alone. If I was to be a monster, I would not be a solitary one. You, who gave me life, must now give me a companion. You owe me this. You have destroyed my one chance of finding fellowship among your species; you must therefore create a new one for me. You must create a female, as hideous and deformed as myself, one who will not recoil from me in horror, but will share my exile and my lot. This is the only condition upon which I will consent to quit the world of men and harm you no more. Refuse, and I will not rest until I have desolated your heart, so that you shall curse the hour of your birth. The choice is yours, but I counsel you to consider it well, for I am armed with a resolution that you cannot comprehend, and my power to inflict misery is now, as you see, proven.

It appeared that he was possessed of considerable wealth, and his Mahometan faith rendered him an object of prejudice and suspicion in a city then fraught with internal strife and a peculiar distrust of foreigners. He was seized upon a pretext, thrown into prison, and condemned to death upon evidence so flimsy and contrived that it shocked the sensibilities of all just men who became acquainted with the particulars of his trial.

Felix had been present at the proceedings, and his soul was fired with indignation at the gross perversion of justice. He saw in the unfortunate Turk not merely a merchant condemned by avarice and bigotry, but a symbol of the tyranny he so abhorred. His attendance at the court was, however, not solely motivated by this abstract love of right; for there, in the gallery, he had beheld the merchant’s daughter, the lovely Arabian, whose dark and expressive eyes were filled with a despair that pierced his very heart. He watched her from day to day, and his pity soon transformed itself into a passion of the most ardent nature. He saw her kneel before the stern judges, her voice, though choked with sobs, pleading with an eloquence that would have moved any but the most hardened of hearts; and when her prayers were met with cold refusal, he resolved in his own mind that he, Felix De Lacey, would become her saviour.

He contrived, through means which required both courage and ingenuity, to gain access to the prison where the condemned man was held. In a low and earnest voice, he declared his purpose. The Turk, at first incredulous, was soon convinced of the young man’s sincerity; for Felix’s noble countenance was the very picture of honour and resolution. A pact was formed between them. The merchant, in his desperation, promised Felix the hand of his daughter, Safie, and a fortune that would secure their future happiness, if only he could be delivered from the ignominy of the scaffold. To Felix, whose heart was already captivated by the Arabian, this offer was a motive far more powerful than any promise of gold. The thought of uniting his destiny with that of the beautiful Safie, of rescuing both her and her father from their dreadful fate, filled him with a heroic ardour.

Preparations for the escape were made with the utmost secrecy and dispatch. In the meantime, Felix found opportunities to communicate with Safie. He could not speak her language, nor she his, but the language of the eyes, and the shared intensity of their situation, formed a powerful bond between them. Safie, as I later learned from the letters she had preserved, was a being of a most singular history. Her mother had been a Christian Arab, who had been enslaved by the Turks but had, through her beauty and intellect, won the heart of Safie’s father. This mother had instilled in her daughter a love of independence and a thirst for knowledge which were wholly at odds with the submissive and secluded life prescribed for women in her father’s country. She had taught her daughter the principles of the Christian religion, and had inspired in her a longing for the more enlightened and free society of Europe, where women were not mere ornaments in a harem but were esteemed as companions and intellectual equals.

Upon her mother’s death, Safie’s father had sought to bind her to a life she detested, but she cherished her mother’s precepts in the secret chambers of her heart and yearned for an opportunity to escape the fate that awaited her in Constantinople. When Felix appeared, a veritable angel of deliverance, handsome, brave, and a native of that very Europe she so longed to inhabit, her heart was given to him at once and for ever. She viewed him as her guide and protector, who would not only save her father’s life but would also lead her to a world of freedom and intellectual delight.

The night appointed for the escape at length arrived. All was darkness and confusion. Felix, with a resolution that never faltered, executed his plan with perfect success. The Turk was freed from his chains and hurried out of Paris. I need not detail the perils of their flight; suffice it to say that they reached the frontiers of France in safety and crossed into Italy, taking refuge in the city of Leghorn. The merchant was now free, but his heart, as it soon became apparent, was a vessel of deceit and ingratitude. While they awaited a favourable opportunity to embark for some obscure port in the Ottoman dominions, news reached them which threw all their plans into disarray and precipitated the ruin of my unhappy protectors.

The government of France, having discovered the escape of their prisoner, was thrown into a state of high indignation. A strict inquiry was launched, and the part which Felix had played in the affair was soon brought to light. The full weight of their vengeance fell not upon the absent Felix, but upon the innocent and unsuspecting family he had left behind in Paris. The venerable De Lacey, whose blindness should have shielded him from harm, and the gentle Agatha, were seized as hostages for the state. They were thrown into prison, and the whole of their fortune was confiscated by the very laws Felix had sought to see justly administered.

When this dreadful intelligence reached Felix in Leghorn, his consternation was absolute. He was torn between his love for Safie and his duty to his suffering family. In this agony of indecision, the true character of Safie’s father was revealed. The treacherous Turk, seeing that his connection with Felix could now only bring him further danger and no advantage, for the De Lacey family was now as poor as himself, determined to break his promise. He had all along viewed the proposed marriage of his daughter to a Christian with abhorrence; he had consented to it only as a means to save his life. Now that he was safe, he endeavoured to compel Safie to prepare for their imminent departure to Constantinople, where he intended to immure her in his seraglio.

But the spirit of Safie was not one to be so easily crushed. She was filled with a righteous anger at her father’s duplicity and with a profound grief for the misfortunes of her noble lover. She secretly gained knowledge of Felix’s plan to return to Paris and surrender himself to the authorities in order to save his father and sister. Before he could depart, however, a milder sentence was passed upon his family: they were condemned to perpetual exile from their native country and stripped of all their rank and possessions. They were to be cast out, penniless and dishonoured.

This news, while it saved Felix from the necessity of surrendering himself, sealed the fate of his family. He immediately took leave of the ungrateful Turk, who, without a word of gratitude or remorse, set sail for his homeland. Felix, his heart heavy with sorrow and his pockets empty, travelled to Germany, where his father and sister, upon their release, were to join him. It was there that they found the humble cottage in which I first beheld them, their lives reduced from affluence and honour to the most abject poverty.

Safie, meanwhile, was left in Italy in the care of a single attendant, with a sum of money and some jewels which she had managed to secure. She was horrified by her father’s treachery and resolved never to join him in a land which she regarded as a prison. Her thoughts were all with her beloved Felix. She knew the name of the country to which he had retired, but little else. Yet, with a courage and determination that I could not but admire, she resolved to seek him out. She sold a portion of her jewels to raise funds for her journey, and leaving her attendant, who proved unfaithful and absconded with the remainder of her portable wealth, she set out alone. Her only guide was a map of Germany and the name of the town near which she hoped to find her lover. By a fortunate chance, the woman in whose house she had lodged in Leghorn was a native of the very region to which the De Laceys had been exiled, and she was able to furnish Safie with a more precise direction. It was thus that, after many weeks of weary travel and anxious uncertainty, she arrived at the door of the cottage, bringing with her a joy and a light that for a time dispelled the gloom which had settled upon my protectors.

Here was a history of injustice and persecution, of virtue rewarded with suffering, of love and loyalty shining brightly amidst the darkness of human cruelty and betrayal. I saw in the fate of the De Laceys a mirror of the world’s harshness, and in the character of Felix, a standard of nobility to which I ardently aspired. I learned from his story that to be good was not always to be happy, and that the laws and systems of men were often instruments of oppression rather than protection.

My admiration for the cottagers grew with each new revelation. I saw them not as poor peasants, but as fallen nobility, bearing their unmerited misfortunes with a grace and fortitude that ennobled them far more than their lost titles or wealth ever could have done. I felt their sorrows as my own, and I burned with indignation against the Turk for his base ingratitude and against the French government for its cruel injustice. And in Safie, the lovely, courageous Arabian, I saw the power of love to transcend all barriers of culture, distance, and adversity.

These lessons, so profoundly impressed upon my developing mind, served only to increase the agony of my own condition. For I, too, was an outcast, a victim of a prejudice far deeper and more insurmountable than that which had condemned the Turkish merchant. He was of a different race and religion, but he was still a man. I was something other, a creature for whom there was no name and no place in the world. The De Laceys had suffered, but they had each other. Their love was a fortress against the slings and arrows of outrageous fortune. But I was utterly alone. I had no father to grieve with, no sister to comfort, no lover to inspire me with courage.

The more I learned of the bonds of human society, the more I felt the crushing weight of my own isolation. I saw the gentle interplay of family life, the comfort of shared glances, the solace of a helping hand, and I knew with a certainty that brought tears of anguish to my eyes that these simple joys were for ever denied to me. I was a spectator at the feast of life, doomed to peer through a window at a warmth and a light in which I could never share. My heart, which had been so full of a nascent love for these good people, began to harbour a new and terrible feeling: a bitter envy that gnawed at my soul. Why had they, who had once known happiness, been allowed to retain the solace of companionship in their misery, while I, who had known nothing but solitude from the moment of my creation, was condemned to suffer it without end?

These reflections soured the pleasure I took in my secret observations. A deep and painful longing took possession of me. It was no longer enough to watch them from a distance; I yearned, with an intensity that was a torment, to be one of them, to be received into their circle, to hear a single word of kindness addressed to me, to feel for a fleeting moment the touch of a friendly hand. I fantasized that I might, through some great service, win their gratitude and overcome their initial revulsion at my appearance. I imagined revealing myself to the blind old man first, for he could not see my deformity. I would win his heart with my words, with the gentle and benevolent feelings which I now knew how to express. I would tell him my story, and he, in his wisdom and compassion, would surely pity me. He would then prepare his children for my arrival, and they, trusting in their father’s judgment, would learn to look past my hideous exterior and see the loving heart within.

This plan became my single obsession, the one ray of hope in the darkness of my existence. Day after day, I rehearsed the speech I would make to the old man, refining my words, modulating my voice, striving to imbue it with all the pathos and sincerity of my wretched condition. I waited for the perfect opportunity, for a day when the old man would be alone in the cottage, that I might put my desperate gamble to the test. The fate of my entire existence, I felt, hung upon the outcome of that single, momentous interview. It was to be the turning point of my life: either I would be received into the arms of fellowship and love, or I would be cast out for ever into a despair so black and so profound that it could only end in a paroxysm of hatred and revenge. The suspense of this waiting was an agony in itself, yet it was an agony mingled with a feverish, almost painful hope, a hope that was soon to be extinguished in the most cruel and decisive manner imaginable. I did not yet know it, but my education in the ways of man was far from complete; I had yet to learn the most bitter lesson of all.

You must create a female for me with whom I can live in the interchange of those sympathies necessary for my being. This you must do, and in this one act of justice you will repay the debt you owe me for my miserable existence and extinguish the flame of vengeance that now consumes my heart. I do not ask for a soul to be joined with mine in the eyes of your God, nor for a partner in the society of men, from which I am eternally outcast. I ask only for a creature of my own kind, as deformed and horrible as myself, who will not recoil from me in terror, but will see in my form a reflection of her own, and in my heart a companion to her solitude.

Your countenance, my creator, became a mask of horror and detestation. You sprung from your seat, your voice choked with a rage that rendered you for a moment speechless. When at last you found utterance, your words were a torrent of execration.

“Never!” you cried, your hands clenched and your eyes blazing with a fury I had not yet witnessed. “Never! I will not create another like you, to join with you in the desolation of the world. Shall I release upon the earth a she-devil to mate with you, and to propagate a race of demons that would make a hell of this fair globe? Begone! The very thought is a torment, and your request an insult to all that is sacred. I will not do it.”

Your refusal, though I had in some measure anticipated it, fell upon my soul like the eternal frost of the glacier on which we stood. Yet my despair was not so complete as to silence the arguments which reason and my own desperate need supplied. I did not move from my place, but allowed the first storm of your passion to subside before I spoke again, my voice low and imbued with a gravity that I hoped might compel your attention.

“You are in the wrong,” I said, “and your arguments are as unjust as your initial abandonment of me. I am malicious because I am miserable; am I not shunned and hated by all mankind? You, my creator, would tear me to pieces and triumph; remember that, and tell me why I should pity man more than he pities me? You would not call it murder if you could precipitate me into one of those ice rifts and destroy my frame, the work of your own hands. Shall I respect man when he contemns me? Let him live with me in the interchange of kindness, and instead of injury I would bestow every benefit upon him with a superfluity of benevolence that would astonish you. But that cannot be; the human senses are insurmountable barriers to our union. Yet my heart yearns for sympathy and companionship. I am alone, and you, my maker, are the cause of that solitude. Grant my prayer in this one instance, and I will be satisfied. I and my companion will depart from the regions of man; we shall seek the vast wilds of South America. My food is not that of man; I do not destroy the lamb and the kid to glut my appetite; acorns and berries afford me sufficient nourishment. My companion will be of the same nature as myself and will be content with the same fare. We shall make our bed of dried leaves; the sun will be our fire, and the running stream our drink. The picture I present to you is peaceful and human, and you must feel that you could deny it only in the wantonness of power and cruelty. Pitiless as you have been towards me, I now see compassion in your eyes; let me seize the favourable moment and persuade you to promise what I so ardently desire.”

“You propose,” you replied, with a sneer that twisted your features into a semblance of my own hated visage, “to fly from the habitations of man, to dwell in deserts where your monstrous form will be concealed. But I know your nature. You are eloquent and persuasive now, but one of your race, a creature of your own desires and passions, would be a far different being. You might be bound by a compact, but she would not. She, who would be my creation but not my pupil, might refuse to comply with a bargain made before her existence. She might have a will of her own, and a hatred for you, her intended companion. What then? Would you not turn your fury upon her, and then, in your doubled misery, upon the whole of mankind? Or worse, far worse, she might take delight in her own evil, and find in you a partner for murder and devastation. You two might hate each other, but you would be united in your hatred of all others. No, I will not be the creator of such a calamity.”

“How is this?” I exclaimed. “You shudder at the thought of future evil, yet you are unmoved by the palpable misery that stands before you! You speak of what she might be, of a will I cannot predict. And what of my will? Did you consider that when you cast me out? I was benevolent and good; misery made me a fiend. Make me happy, and I shall again be virtuous. Can you deny that there is justice in my plea? We should live in a world of our own, and the productions of our hands would be for our own sustenance. The birds and beasts of the forest would be our only society. I swear to you, by the earth which I inhabit, and by you that made me, that with the companion you bestow I will quit the neighbourhood of man and dwell in the most savage of places. My evil passions will have lost their sting; I shall have no cause for them. My life, until now a series of torments, will become tolerable, and in time, I may even dare to hope, peaceful. My descent from the mountain was not as the ascent had been; then, I was a creature of pure rage, a vessel of vengeance whose heart was as frozen as the ice beneath my feet. Now, a strange warmth pervaded my being, a nascent hope that transfigured the desolate landscape before me. The world, which for so long had appeared only as a theatre of my misery, now held the promise of a future I had never dared to conceive. I was no longer a solitary accident, a hideous mockery of life; I was to be the Adam of a new race, and an Eve, formed like myself, was to be my companion in exile. This thought was a balm to my tortured spirit, and I traversed the treacherous glaciers and rocky defiles with a lightness in my step that belied my immense frame. The very air seemed less sharp, the sun less mocking in its brilliance.

I journeyed eastward, away from the icy peaks of Montanvert, and descended into the verdant valleys of Germany. My former caution returned to me, but it was no longer born of a cowering fear; it was now a calculated necessity, a means to preserve the fragile peace I had purchased with my threats. I was a guardian of my own future happiness, and I would not risk it for any fleeting interaction with the world of men. I travelled only by night, resting in the deepest recesses of forests or in abandoned shepherd’s huts during the day. My senses, ever acute, were my constant sentinels. I learned the patterns of the moon and the stars, and they became my guides and my only companions. The rustle of a leaf, the snap of a twig, the distant baying of a farmer’s dog; all these were noted and understood, woven into the silent tapestry of my nocturnal existence.

I sustained myself as I had always done, on berries, nuts, and roots, and by the occasional capture of some small, unwary animal. My tastes were simple, my needs few. The greatest of my appetites was not for food or warmth, but for the fulfillment of your solemn oath. I knew that you would first return to Geneva, and so I bent my course in that direction, not to menace your family, but to remain the unseen observer of your actions, the spectral creditor to your terrible debt. I skirted the towns and villages, a fleeting phantom in the periphery of the human world. I saw the cheerful glow of cottage windows, heard the distant strains of music and laughter, and though these sights still pierced my heart with a familiar pang of longing, the pain was now mingled with anticipation. Soon, I thought, I too shall have a hearth to share; soon, a voice will answer mine not with shrieks of terror, but with words of understanding and affection.

Weeks turned into a month, and I found myself lingering in the dark woods that bordered the lands of your birth. From the crest of a hill, I could sometimes discern the distant glimmer of the lake and the spires of the city. I watched, and I waited. My patience, a faculty I had learned in the long, dark months of my early existence, was now my chief occupation. It was during this period of vigilant stillness that I made a discovery which was to afford me new and profound matter for reflection.

Driven by a great storm one night to seek shelter in a more substantial structure than my usual copses of pine, I came upon the ruins of an ancient monastery. It was a melancholy place, its stone walls crumbling and overgrown with ivy, its great bell tower a jagged silhouette against the tempestuous sky. Most of the structure was open to the elements, but I found one small cloistered library, its roof only partially collapsed, which offered some protection from the driving rain. It was here, amidst the decay of piety and learning, that I found a new treasure. A fire had, many years before, ravaged this portion of the building, yet some books, sheltered in a stone recess, had been spared the worst of the flames. They were scorched and water-damaged, their bindings cracked and their pages stained, but to me they were more precious than any gold.

With the first light of dawn, I examined my prize. There were three volumes in a state that I could, with care, render legible. The first was a copy of Plutarch’s _Lives_, translated into the French tongue. The second, a small book of German poetry. The third, to my astonishment and delight, was a treatise on natural philosophy, filled with diagrams of the heavens and the earth, and speculations upon the very nature of matter and of life. My education, which I owed to the kindness of the unwitting De Laceys, was now to be continued in this lonely ruin, with the ghosts of forgotten monks as my silent tutors.

For many weeks, the ruined monastery was my university. By day, I would pore over the brittle pages, and by night, I would wander the woods, my mind wrestling with the vast new ideas that had been presented to it. From Plutarch, I learned of the founders of states and the lawgivers of antiquity. I saw in the lives of these great men the very virtues and vices which Volney had described. I thrilled at the noble severity of Lycurgus and the wise statesmanship of Solon; I felt my heart swell with admiration for their patriotism and their capacity for self-sacrifice. Yet I also saw their ambition, their cruelty, and the terrible wars they waged. Again the question returned to me: what was this creature, man, whose history was a chronicle of such glorious heights and such deplorable depths? These were the men esteemed by the world, the very pinnacle of their species. I compared my own state to theirs. They built cities; I hid in ruins. They commanded armies; I fled from the sight of a single child. They were remembered for their deeds, their names echoing through centuries; I had no name, and my only deed had been to inspire horror and disgust. The contrast filled me with a despair so profound that I would sometimes cast the book aside and emit a groan of utter anguish that seemed to shake the very stones around me.

But if Plutarch elevated and then crushed my spirit with these monumental comparisons, it was in the verses of the poet that my own soul found its truest, most painful echo. I laboured mightily with the German tongue, and though my progress was slow, I was rewarded with an understanding that went beyond mere language. Here were not the grand affairs of state and war, but the interior landscapes of a solitary heart. The poet spoke of the sublime beauty of nature, of the melancholy of twilight, of the unutterable longing for a kindred spirit, of a sorrow that seemed to emanate from the very fabric of existence. His words were a mirror to my own inarticulate feelings. I wept, not with Safie over the fate of fallen empires, but for myself, and for the beauty of a world I could see and feel but never truly join. I learned that my wretchedness was not unique in its quality, only in its cause and its degree. Others had felt this isolation, this sense of being an exile in the world; but they were men, and could clothe their sorrow in beautiful language, whereas I was a monster, and could only express mine in groans and rage.

The book of natural philosophy, meanwhile, opened yet another field of wonder. It spoke of the laws that governed the stars, the composition of the air I breathed, and the intricate machinery of living things. But it was a work of a former age, and as I read of the quest for the elixir of life and the philosopher’s stone, and of the generation of life from inanimate matter, a new and terrible understanding began to dawn in my mind. I saw that your creation of me, which I had hitherto regarded as a unique and miraculous event, was perhaps but the culmination of the dreams and labours of men such as these. You were their heir, the one who had succeeded where they had failed. But in their writings, this pursuit was framed as a noble quest for knowledge, a desire to elevate the human condition. Where, in your work, was the nobility? You had animated a body, but had you not done so with the reckless and selfish ardour of a child playing with fire, with no thought for the soul you had imprisoned within your monstrous creation? You had sought to become a god, but had behaved as a demon, abandoning your progeny to a fate of unparalleled misery. These reflections did not diminish my desire for the companion you had promised; on the contrary, they intensified it, for I saw that my only hope of finding any semblance of the affection and duty described in my other books lay not with my creator, but with a being fashioned from the same clay as myself.

One evening, as I sat concealed in my customary thicket, I observed a scene that impressed itself upon me more deeply than any page I had ever read. Not far from my position stood a small, neat cottage, and in a window illuminated by a single candle, an old man sat reading. He was alone, and his face, which I could see quite clearly, was etched with the lines of care and intellectual labour. He was surrounded by books, much like myself in my ruin, and I felt an immediate and powerful kinship with this solitary scholar. I saw him sigh and pass a hand over his tired eyes, and my heart ached with a sympathy that was almost painful. Here, I thought, is one who understands the loneliness of a life spent in contemplation. He, like me, finds his companions in the silent pages of the dead.

But as I watched, the door to the room opened, and a young woman entered, carrying a tray with a steaming cup. She placed it gently on the table beside him, and then, with a look of ineffable tenderness, she placed her hand upon his shoulder. The old man looked up, and his tired face was transformed by a smile of pure affection. He said some gentle words, and she laughed softly, a sound like the chiming of a silver bell. They spoke for a few moments, their voices a low murmur that did not reach my ears, but their meaning was as clear as if they had shouted it across the fields. It was the language of love, of care, of familial bonds. He was solitary, yet not forsaken; I was solitude itself, an island of misery in the great ocean of existence.

The agony that this simple scene inflicted upon me was greater than any physical torment. I fled from the spot, my breast heaving with a storm of emotions I could not control. I ran, heedless of my path, until I collapsed at the foot of a great oak, the very tree that had been blasted by lightning and had first inspired your fatal curiosity. Here, in this place of genesis, I gave vent to my despair. All my learning, all my newfound knowledge of history and poetry, served only to sharpen the spears of my anguish. It was one thing to know I was alone; it was another to understand, in all its devastating clarity, the myriad forms of companionship from which I was forever barred.

This incident solidified my resolve. My hope, which had been a patient, contemplative thing, began to burn with the fire of impatience. The waiting became a new form of torture. I imagined my companion; I pictured her form, her face, the expression in her eyes when she would first behold me. Would she, too, turn from me in horror? The thought was a dagger in my heart, but I cast it out. No, she would be like me. She would understand my ugliness, for she would share it. She would see the sorrow in my eyes and recognize it as her own. Her first words would not be a scream, but a question. Her first touch would not be a blow, but a gesture of communion. We would be a world unto ourselves, and the rejection of mankind would be but a distant rumour, a tale of a foreign land we had no desire to visit.

I abandoned my ruined monastery and its precious books and began to follow your trail more actively. I learned from the gossip of travellers and the talk of peasants in the fields that you had departed from Geneva, that you had journeyed to England in the company of a friend. This news filled me with a grim satisfaction. England, I knew, was at the forefront of the very natural philosophy I had been studying. It was there you would gather your materials, there you would begin your secret and abhorred task. Your journey was the signal for mine to commence in earnest.

I made my way across France, a dark pilgrim drawn by the lodestar of your promise. I crossed the channel by stowing away in the hold of a small vessel, a miserable and terrifying passage during which I was surrounded by the sounds and smells of men, yet as isolated as if I had been on the moon. Once on English soil, I felt I was drawing nearer to the consummation of my destiny. I followed you to London, a city whose immensity and ceaseless activity were a source of constant wonder and dread. I was a monster in the heart of the greatest of human hives, yet my invisibility was more complete here than in any wilderness. I was but one more shadow in a city of a million shadows.

From a distance, I was your keeper. I saw you walk the streets, your brow furrowed with a constant torment that I, your creation, had etched there. I saw you with your friend, and the sight of your easy companionship, a thing you so cruelly denied to me, stoked the embers of my resentment. Do not think that I was ever far. When you looked over your shoulder with a start, it was my presence you felt. When you started from your sleep in a cold sweat, it was my face that haunted your dreams. I was the spectre of your conscience, the living embodiment of your oath.

And now, I have learned that you have left your friend and travelled north, towards the desolate extremities of Scotland. I know your purpose. I know the destination you seek. The time of waiting is almost at an end. The Orkneys. The name is a promise and a command. It is there that my Eve will be born, there on a remote and windswept shore, far from the prying eyes of the world. It is there that my long night of solitude will finally meet its dawn.

I am coming, creator. I am following you north. The hope that was once a pale and fragile seedling has now grown into a vast and demanding tree that fills my entire being. Do not falter. Do not delay. Fulfill your promise, for my patience has worn thin, and the philosopher and the poet within me are once more in danger of being consumed by the beast. Complete your work, and I shall take my companion and vanish from your life and from the memory of man forever. But if you fail me, if you betray this last and only hope of a miserable being, then I swear to you by the hell of my own existence that I will become the scourge you have always feared, and the tale of our mutual ruin shall be the last and only history I will ever learn.
