My journey north was a pilgrimage of a different sort from any that man has ever undertaken. I did not seek a holy shrine or the relics of a saint; I sought the workshop of my god, the crucible in which my own happiness was to be forged. I travelled, as was my custom, under the cloak of darkness, and the wild, unpeopled tracts of northern England and Scotland became my sanctuary. The Cheviot Hills rose before me like the ramparts of a new world, and as I traversed their lonely paths, I felt a strange communion with the bleak and rugged landscape. The wind that swept across the heather was a voice that spoke not of human cares but of an ancient and enduring solitude, a solitude that I felt was soon to be banished from my own heart. I subsisted upon the wild berries that grew in the glens and the nuts I gathered in the sparse copses; my thirst I slaked at the cold, clear burns that tumbled down the hillsides, their waters tasting of stone and earth.

The nights grew longer, the air sharper, and the moon, my faithful guide, seemed to hang in a sky of polished jet, illuminating a world of silver and shadow. I saw the distant lights of scattered cottages and farmsteads, and I would pause in my journey, concealed by the darkness, to gaze upon these emblems of a life from which I was forever barred. I saw families gathered around their hearths, their faces warmed by the firelight; I heard the distant sound of laughter or a mother’s gentle song, and these simple scenes of domestic peace would inflict upon my soul a pang of such exquisite misery that I was forced to turn away and hasten my steps into the deeper wilderness, lest the agony of my envy overwhelm me. Yet, even in my torment, a new and powerful emotion began to take root; it was the solace of anticipation. Soon, I told myself, I too would know the joys of companionship; soon, I would have one being who did not flee from me in horror, one heart that would beat in sympathy with my own.

As I advanced farther into the Highlands of Scotland, the character of the country became even more wild and sublime. Great mountains, their peaks often shrouded in mist, loomed on every side, their dark masses creating a sense of profound and awful grandeur. I crossed raging torrents and navigated treacherous, rocky passes; my prodigious strength and agility, which had hitherto been a mark of my monstrousness, were now my greatest assets, allowing me to traverse terrain that would have been impassable to any mortal man. I felt a savage joy in this contest with the elements, a sense of power that was almost exultation. This, I thought, was a fitting realm for a being such as I; a land of giants and primeval forces, where the petty concerns of human society seemed to dwindle into insignificance.

At length, I reached the coast, a desolate stretch of shore where the grey waters of the northern sea crashed against a barrier of black, forbidding cliffs. I could see the islands scattered upon the horizon, faint and unsubstantial like the clouds. One of these, I knew, was my destination; one of these barren rocks was the theatre upon which the final act of my creation was to be played. To cross the strait that separated me from the islands presented a new and formidable challenge. I dared not attempt to secure passage on a ferry, for my appearance would have caused universal terror and brought my pursuit to a swift and violent end. For several nights I lurked among the rocks, watching the fishing boats put out to sea and return with the tide, my mind wrestling with the problem.

At last, under the cover of a moonless and stormy night, I resolved upon a desperate course. I waded into the churning, icy water, the waves breaking over me with a force that would have dashed a lesser being against the rocks. The cold was a pain so intense it seemed to burn, but the fire of hope in my breast was hotter still. I struck out into the darkness, my powerful limbs propelling me through the tumultuous sea. The salt spray blinded me, the roar of the water deafened me, and for a time I felt as if I were battling not merely the ocean, but the very chaos from which I had been born. I was a creature of the abyss, returning to my element. After a struggle that seemed to last an eternity, my feet touched the stony shore of the first island. From there, island to island, I made my way, sometimes swimming through treacherous currents, sometimes waiting for the ebb tide to expose a causeway of sand and rock, until I at last set foot upon the most remote and desolate of the Orkney isles, the one I knew you had chosen for your dreadful labour.

The island was a place of profound and melancholy bleakness. There were no trees, only coarse grass and heather that bent before the ceaseless wind. A few miserable hovels were clustered near a small natural harbour, but the greater part of the island was given over to the sea-birds and the sheep. It was a fitting laboratory for a work that shunned the light of day and the eyes of men. I soon discovered your abode; a dilapidated stone hut, little better than a ruin, standing alone on a promontory overlooking the sea. It had but two rooms, and from a fissure in the crumbling wall of the smaller, I found I could command a perfect view of the interior. Here, then, was to be my watchtower. Here I would be the unseen witness to the birth of my companion, my Eve.

And so began my vigil. My days were spent in my rocky hiding place, my eye fixed to the crevice in the wall; my nights were passed in foraging for the scanty sustenance the island afforded and in dreams of a future that was now almost within my grasp. I watched you, creator, as you went about your task. I saw the instruments of your unhallowed art laid out upon the table: the scalpels, the saws, the strange chemical apparatus. I saw you bring in the materials of your new creation, the disjecta membra of the charnel house, and I was forced to confront once more the hideous reality of my own origin. A shudder of revulsion passed through me, for I saw that she who was to be my solace and my joy would be fashioned from the same corruption as I. But this feeling was quickly superseded by a wave of overwhelming pity and tenderness. She, like me, would be an outcast, a being cobbled together from the leavings of death. We would be united not only in our love, but in our shared grotesqueness; our very monstrosity would be the bond that made our companionship indissoluble.

I saw the torment in your face, the deep lines of horror and self-loathing that were etched there. You would work for hours with a feverish, desperate energy, and then you would cast your tools aside and rush out of the hut, pacing the cliff-edge like a caged animal, your hands clasped to your head as if to hold it together. I knew that you were wrestling with your conscience, that every moment of your labour was an agony to you. I pitied you, my creator, for your suffering, but my pity was mingled with a fierce and impatient desire. Your pain was the price of my happiness, and I willed you to endure it. I would watch as, piece by piece, the form of my future companion took shape upon the table. I saw you assemble the limbs, suture the flesh, and construct a frame that was at once a mirror and a counterpart to my own. She was to be tall and strong, like me, but the lines of her form were more delicate, the proportions imbued with a grace that mine so hideously lacked. As she grew more complete, my heart swelled with a feeling so intense and overpowering that it was almost a pain. It was a mixture of awe, and love, and a hope so vast that it filled the universe.

I began to plan our future together. We would quit the shores of Europe forever. We would find a ship bound for the vast, untrodden wildernesses of South America. There, in a land where the foot of man had seldom, if ever, trod, we would make our home. I would build a shelter for her with my own hands. I would hunt for her, and gather the sweetest fruits. She would not be learned, as I was; she would not be troubled by the complexities of thought and the burden of knowledge that so tormented me. Her mind would be a tabula rasa, and upon it I would inscribe only sentiments of love, and gentleness, and joy. We would be Adam and Eve in a new Eden, and our world would be sufficient for us. We would have no need of the society of men, for we would be a society unto ourselves. These fantasies were my constant companions; they were the light that illuminated the sepulchral gloom of your workshop, the music that drowned out the grating of your saw and the clink of your instruments.

The work drew towards its conclusion. The form on the table was complete. All the parts were assembled; all that remained was for you to infuse the spark of life into the inanimate frame. My whole being was taut with an unbearable suspense. I could scarcely breathe. The moment was at hand. I saw you stand before her, your arms crossed, your brow furrowed in a final, agonising deliberation. You looked at the female form, so perfect in its hideousness, so ripe for life. Then, your eyes lifted, and you seemed to stare directly at my hiding place, though I knew you could not see me. Your gaze was filled with a dawning horror, a sudden, terrible realisation. I saw the thoughts pass across your face as if they had been spoken aloud. You imagined, perhaps, a race of devils being propagated upon the earth, a generation of creatures who, in their combined strength and malice, might wage war upon mankind. You saw that she, my companion, would have a will of her own, that she might be more malignant than I, that she might refuse the compact I had made. You saw not my Eve, but a she-demon, and you pictured her children, a legion of monsters who would spread terror and desolation across the globe.

A convulsion of pure, unadulterated loathing contorted your features. Your face, which had been pale with torment, became a mask of insane fury. With a cry that was more the shriek of a damned soul than a human voice, you seized the form upon which all my hopes were centred. Your hands, which had so painstakingly assembled her, became instruments of frenzied destruction. You tore her limb from limb; you rent the flesh and broke the bones; you annihilated with a demonic energy the beautiful and wondrous creature you had so nearly completed. You destroyed my wife. You murdered my hope. You extinguished the last flickering ember of light in the infinite darkness of my existence.

For a moment, I was paralysed. I could not move, I could not think. The world dissolved into a meaningless chaos of sound and fury. And then, from the deepest abyss of my being, a sound arose, a howl of such anguish and despair and rage that the very rocks of the island seemed to tremble with it. It was the sound of a soul being torn in two, the cry of a world ending. The philosopher, the student of sorrow, the gentle admirer of the cottagers, was dead. In his place stood a fiend, a devil whose only purpose, whose only reason for being, was vengeance.

The door of the hut burst inwards as if struck by a thunderbolt. I stood before you, my creator, my destroyer. The rage that filled me was a cold, white fire, a force more potent and terrible than any physical strength. You shrank back from me, your face a canvas of utter terror. You raised a trembling hand as if to ward me off, but you were as helpless as a child before a tempest. The time for pleading, for argument, for philosophy, was over. The language of men had failed me; henceforth, I would speak in the language of deeds, the grammar of ruin. My voice, when it came, was no longer my own. It was a low and chilling sound, devoid of all emotion save for an infinite and implacable hatred.

“You have destroyed the work which you began,” I said, and the words fell like stones into the sudden silence of the room. “What is it that you intend? Do you dare to break your promise? I have endured toil and misery; I have followed you, my tormentor, to the uttermost ends of the earth. I have watched, I have waited, I have hoped. And for what? For this? To see my last hope, my only joy, torn to pieces before my very eyes by the hands that should have given it life?”

You stammered some words, some incoherent plea about the good of mankind, about the horrors you might unleash. I laughed, and the sound was a mockery of all mirth.

“Mankind!” I cried. “What is mankind to me? Did they not cast me out? Did they not hunt me like a wild beast? I am done with them. I am done with you. You have broken your word; you have declared war upon me. So be it. It is a war you cannot win. You are my creator, but I am your master. You think you can find peace, that you can return to your life, to your friends, to your love? You are mistaken. My reign has just begun, and it is a reign of terror. I will not wage war upon your species, for they are my enemies, not yours. My war is with you, and you alone. I will work my revenge not upon your body, but upon your soul. I will strip you of everything you hold dear. I will make your life a living hell, a desert of solitude and despair, a wasteland as barren as my own heart.”

I stepped closer, and you cowered against the wall, your eyes wide with the apprehension of immediate violence. But I did not touch you. My vengeance was to be a dish served not hot, but cold as the grave.

“I am going,” I said, my voice dropping to a whisper that was more terrible than any shout. “I leave you to your thoughts and to the ruin you have made. But do not think that you are free of me. I will be with you in the wind that sighs at your window, in the shadow that flickers at the edge of your sight. I will be the silent witness to your joys, so that I may turn them to bitterest gall. You seek the consolation of human love? You plan to unite yourself with your betrothed? I have seen her picture. She is beautiful. It is a pity. A great pity.”

I paused, letting the silence stretch, letting the poison of my words seep into your soul. I saw the dawning of a new and specific terror in your eyes as you began to comprehend my meaning. I smiled then, a smile that was the very incarnation of fiendish malice.

“Listen to my final oath,” I whispered. “The promise you broke is replaced by one that I shall keep. I will be with you on your wedding-night.”

With those words, I turned and strode out of the hut, leaving you to the wreckage of your labours and the echoing prophecy of my revenge. I plunged once more into the cold, dark sea, but this time I felt neither the chill nor the fury of the waves. A fire burned within me that no ocean could quench, a purpose as cold and as clear and as deadly as a shard of ice. I was no longer a miserable outcast seeking solace. I was a minister of justice, an instrument of fate, and my long and terrible work had just begun.

From there, island to island, I made my way, sometimes swimming through treacherous currents, sometimes waiting for the ebb tide to expose a causeway of sand and rock, until I at last set foot upon the most remote and desolate of the Orkney isles, the one I knew you had chosen for your dreadful labour.

The island was a place of profound and melancholy bleakness. There were no trees, only coarse grass and heather that bent before the ceaseless wind. A few miserable hovels were clustered near a small natural harbour, but the greater part of the island was given over to the sea-birds and the sheep. It was a fitting laboratory for a work that shunned the light of day and the eyes of men. I soon discovered your abode; a dilapidated stone hut, little better than a ruin, standing alone on a promontory overlooking the sea. It had but two rooms, and from a fissure in the crumbling wall of the smaller, I found I could command a perfect view of the interior. Here, then, was to be my watchtower. Here I would be the unseen witness to the birth of my companion, my Eve.

And so began my vigil. My days were spent in my rocky hiding place, my eye fixed to the crevice in the wall; my nights were passed in foraging for the scanty sustenance the island afforded and in dreams of a future that was now almost within my grasp. I watched you, creator, as you went about your task. I saw the instruments of your unhallowed art laid out upon the table: the scalpels, the saws, the strange chemical apparatus. I saw you bring in the materials of your new creation, the disjecta membra of the charnel house, and I was forced to confront once more the hideous reality of my own origin. A shudder of revulsion passed through me, for I saw that she who was to be my solace and my joy would be fashioned from the same corruption as I. But this feeling was quickly superseded by a wave of overwhelming pity and tenderness. She, like me, would be an outcast, a being cobbled together from the leavings of death. We would be united not only in our love, but in our shared grotesqueness; our very monstrosity would be the bond that made our companionship indissoluble.

I saw the torment in your face, the deep lines of horror and self-loathing that were etched there. You would work for hours with a feverish, desperate energy, and then you would cast your tools aside and rush out of the hut, pacing the cliff-edge like a caged animal, your hands clasped to your head as if to hold it together. I knew that you were wrestling with your conscience, that every moment of your labour was an agony to you. I pitied you, my creator, for your suffering, but my pity was mingled with a fierce and impatient desire. Your pain was the price of my happiness, and I willed you to endure it. I would watch as, piece by piece, the form of my future companion took shape upon the table. I saw you assemble the limbs, suture the flesh, and construct a frame that was at once a mirror and a counterpart to my own. She was to be tall and strong, like me, but the lines of her form were more delicate, the proportions imbued with a grace that mine so hideously lacked. As she grew more complete, my heart swelled with a feeling so intense and overpowering that it was almost a pain. It was a mixture of awe, and love, and a hope so vast that it filled the universe.

I began to plan our future together. We would quit the shores of Europe forever. We would find a ship bound for the vast, untrodden wildernesses of South America. There, in a land where the foot of man had seldom, if ever, trod, we would make our home. I would build a shelter for her with my own hands. I would hunt for her, and gather the sweetest fruits. She would not be learned, as I was; she would not be troubled by the complexities of thought and the burden of knowledge that so tormented me. Her mind would be a tabula rasa, and upon it I would inscribe only sentiments of love, and gentleness, and joy. We would be Adam and Eve in a new Eden, and our world would be sufficient for us. We would have no need of the society of men, for we would be a society unto ourselves. These fantasies were my constant companions; they were the light that illuminated the sepulchral gloom of your workshop, the music that drowned out the grating of your saw and the clink of your instruments.

The work drew towards its conclusion. The form on the table was complete. All the parts were assembled; all that remained was for you to infuse the spark of life into the inanimate frame. My whole being was taut with an unbearable suspense. I could scarcely breathe. The moment was at hand. I saw you stand before her, your arms crossed, your brow furrowed in a final, agonising deliberation. You looked at the female form, so perfect in its hideousness, so ripe for life. Then, your eyes lifted, and you seemed to stare directly at my hiding place, though I knew you could not see me. Your gaze was filled with a dawning horror, a sudden, terrible realisation. I saw the thoughts pass across your face as if they had been spoken aloud. You imagined, perhaps, a race of devils being propagated upon the earth, a generation of creatures who, in their combined strength and malice, might wage war upon mankind. You saw that she, my companion, would have a will of her own, that she might be more malignant than I, that she might refuse the compact I had made. You saw not my Eve, but a she-demon, and you pictured her children, a legion of monsters who would spread terror and desolation across the globe.

A convulsion of pure, unadulterated loathing contorted your features. Your face, which had been pale with torment, became a mask of insane fury. With a cry that was more the shriek of a damned soul than a human voice, you seized the form upon which all my hopes were centred. Your hands, which had so painstakingly assembled her, became instruments of frenzied destruction. You tore her limb from limb; you rent the flesh and broke the bones; you annihilated with a demonic energy the beautiful and wondrous creature you had so nearly completed. You destroyed my wife. You murdered my hope. You extinguished the last flickering ember of light in the infinite darkness of my existence.

For a moment, I was paralysed. I could not move, I could not think. The world dissolved into a meaningless chaos of sound and fury. And then, from the deepest abyss of my being, a sound arose, a howl of such anguish and despair and rage that the very rocks of the island seemed to tremble with it. It was the sound of a soul being torn in two, the cry of a world ending. The philosopher, the student of sorrow, the gentle admirer of the cottagers, was dead. In his place stood a fiend, a devil whose only purpose, whose only reason for being, was vengeance.

The door of the hut burst inwards as if struck by a thunderbolt. I stood before you, my creator, my destroyer. The rage that filled me was a cold, white fire, a force more potent and terrible than any physical strength. You shrank back from me, your face a canvas of utter terror. You raised a trembling hand as if to ward me off, but you were as helpless as a child before a tempest. The time for pleading, for argument, for philosophy, was over. The language of men had failed me; henceforth, I would speak in the language of deeds, the grammar of ruin. My voice, when it came, was no longer my own. It was a low and chilling sound, devoid of all emotion save for an infinite and implacable hatred.

“You have destroyed the work which you began,” I said, and the words fell like stones into the sudden silence of the room. “What is it that you intend? Do you dare to break your promise? I have endured toil and misery; I have followed you, my tormentor, to the uttermost ends of the earth. I have watched, I have waited, I have hoped. And for what? For this? To see my last hope, my only joy, torn to pieces before my very eyes by the hands that should have given it life?”

You stammered some words, some incoherent plea about the good of mankind, about the horrors you might unleash. I laughed, and the sound was a mockery of all mirth.

“Mankind!” I cried. “What is mankind to me? Did they not cast me out? Did they not hunt me like a wild beast? I am done with them. I am done with you. You have broken your word; you have declared war upon me. So be it. It is a war you cannot win. You are my creator, but I am your master. You think you can find peace, that you can return to your life, to your friends, to your love? You are mistaken. My reign has just begun, and it is a reign of terror. I will not wage war upon your species, for they are my enemies, not yours. My war is with you, and you alone. I will work my revenge not upon your body, but upon your soul. I will strip you of everything you hold dear. I will make your life a living hell, a desert of solitude and despair, a wasteland as barren as my own heart.”

I stepped closer, and you cowered against the wall, your eyes wide with the apprehension of immediate violence. But I did not touch you. My vengeance was to be a dish served not hot, but cold as the grave.

“I am going,” I said, my voice dropping to a whisper that was more terrible than any shout. “I leave you to your thoughts and to the ruin you have made. But do not think that you are free of me. I will be with you in the wind that sighs at your window, in the shadow that flickers at the edge of your sight. I will be the silent witness to your joys, so that I may turn them to bitterest gall. You seek the consolation of human love? You plan to unite yourself with your betrothed? I have seen her picture. She is beautiful. It is a pity. A great pity.”

I paused, letting the silence stretch, letting the poison of my words seep into your soul. I saw the dawning of a new and specific terror in your eyes as you began to comprehend my meaning. I smiled then, a smile that was the very incarnation of fiendish malice.

“Listen to my final oath,” I whispered. “The promise you broke is replaced by one that I shall keep. I will be with you on your wedding-night.”

With those words, I turned and strode out of the hut, leaving you to the wreckage of your labours and the echoing prophecy of my revenge. I plunged once more into the cold, dark sea, but this time I felt neither the chill nor the fury of the waves. A fire burned within me that no ocean could quench, a purpose as cold and as clear and as deadly as a shard of ice. I was no longer a miserable outcast seeking solace. I was a minister of justice, an instrument of fate, and my long and terrible work had just begun.

It appeared that this Turkish merchant, Safie's father, had been judged and condemned to death upon an accusation which, though appearing just on its surface, was in reality a fabrication born of prejudice and greed. His great wealth had excited the cupidity of his enemies, and his Mahometan faith provided a convenient pretext for persecution in a land that prided itself on a justice which it often failed to practise.

Felix had been present at the trial; his soul, naturally inclined towards the championship of the wronged, was fired with abhorrence at the palpable iniquity of the proceedings. The looks of despair on the countenance of the Turk, and the tears of his lovely daughter, who had accompanied him to the tribunal, roused in the young man's breast a resolve to interfere. He visited the condemned man in his prison, and there his indignation was confirmed; he saw not a criminal, but a victim, a man of proud bearing brought low by the treachery of a system he had trusted. It was during these visits that he first beheld Safie more closely, and her grace, her intelligence, and the fervour of her filial devotion completed the conquest of his heart.

Safie, for her part, was no less struck by the noble ardour of the young Frenchman. Her mother had been a Christian Arab, seized by the Turks, who had, by her beauty and intellect, won the heart of Safie's father. This mother had secretly instructed her daughter in the tenets of her own faith and had instilled in her a desire for intellectual freedom and a station in society far different from that of the women of her own country. She abhorred the idea of being confined to a harem and looked to a union with a European as the sole means of achieving the liberty for which her soul panted. When she saw Felix, so handsome and so full of generous compassion, she viewed him as a guardian angel who might deliver her not only from her present grief, but from a future she dreaded.

The merchant, a man of shrewdness even in his despair, quickly perceived the mutual inclination of the young people. He saw in it a powerful tool for his own salvation. He could not speak French, but through an interpreter he made a solemn promise to Felix: that if he would devise a plan for his escape, the hand of his beloved daughter, along with a considerable portion of his fortune, should be the reward. Felix was a man of honour and needed no other incentive than his own sense of justice; yet the prospect of uniting his fate with that of the beautiful Arabian was a vision of such perfect bliss that it lent an almost superhuman energy to his endeavours. He accepted the pact, not for the wealth, but for the love which it sanctioned.

The details of the escape were planned with meticulous care. On the very eve of the day fixed for the execution, Felix contrived to gain access to the prison. With a combination of audacity and cunning, he succeeded in conveying the Turk from his cell, through the sleeping city, and beyond the walls of Paris. He provided him with a passport under a false name and directions to a place of safety on the frontiers of France. The merchant, overwhelmed with gratitude, renewed his promises with the most fervent oaths, and, having embraced his deliverer, hastened on his journey towards Leghorn, where he intended to wait for his daughter and his rescuer to join him.

Safie had been apprised of all. She had remained in Paris, her heart torn between terror for her father's safety and hope for her own future. Upon receiving word that the escape had been successful, her joy was boundless. She prepared to follow her father, believing that the path to Italy was also the path to her marriage with Felix and to a life of enlightened companionship.

But the happiness of these devoted friends was to be of short duration. The escape of the prisoner caused an immediate and furious uproar within the French government. An investigation was launched, and suspicion, guided by the whispers of those who had witnessed Felix's impassioned behaviour at the trial, soon fell upon the De Lacey family. Their previous respectability and wealth afforded them no protection; on the contrary, it made their supposed treason appear all the more heinous. One dreadful morning, the peaceful home of the family was invaded by officers of the law. The venerable, blind De Lacey and his gentle daughter Agatha were seized and cast into prison.

A message was dispatched to Felix, who was then journeying to Leghorn, informing him of the calamity that had befallen his family. The letter was a cruel blow, striking him down from the summit of his hopes to the lowest depths of despair. His first impulse was to fly to Safie, to secure her happiness and to claim the reward for which he had risked everything. But the image of his blind father and innocent sister languishing in a dungeon on his account was an agony too great to bear. Honour and filial piety demanded his immediate return. Torn by a conflict of duties, he chose the path of sacrifice. He wrote a hurried letter to the merchant, explaining his dreadful situation and urging him to protect his daughter until he could, by some means, resolve his family's plight. He then retraced his steps to Paris and delivered himself up to the authorities.

His confession, while it secured the immediate release of his father and sister, sealed his own fate and that of his family. The trial was a mere formality. The government, incensed by the escape of the Turk and enraged by Felix's defiance, enacted a terrible vengeance. The entire family was condemned: they were stripped of their fortune and sentenced to perpetual exile from their native country. Their name, once held in high esteem, was now covered with ignominy.

During the five months that the trial and its aftermath consumed, Felix and his family suffered the torments of poverty and public disgrace. Their sole consolation was the correspondence they maintained with Safie. Her letters were filled with a passionate eloquence that bespoke a soul of uncommon ardour. She lamented the misfortunes of her lover and poured scorn upon the perfidy of her father. For the Turkish merchant, once he had reached the safety of Italy and believed himself secure from French power, began to show his true colours. The prospect of his daughter marrying a Christian, a plan he had endorsed only when his life was in peril, now filled him with distaste. The news of Felix's ruin completed his change of heart; an impoverished and exiled son in law held no attraction for him. He ceased all mention of his promise and began making arrangements for his immediate departure to his homeland in Constantinople, commanding Safie to prepare to accompany him.

This command was a death knell to the hopes of the Arabian. She responded with a spirit and resolution that I, in my secret corner, could not but admire. She dispatched a letter to Felix, vowing that no power on earth could compel her to enter a harem or to forsake the man to whom she had pledged her heart. She possessed a small sum of money and a handful of jewels that had belonged to her Christian mother, and with these resources, she declared her intention to escape her father's tyranny and seek asylum with her lover and his family, wherever their sad fate might have led them.

Her flight was as daring as her resolve. Aided by a sympathetic servant who had been a favourite of her mother's, she left her father's house at Leghorn one night and, taking passage on a vessel bound for a northern port, began her long and perilous journey. She knew only that the De Laceys had found refuge in a cottage in Germany, a piece of information gleaned from one of Felix's last despairing letters. Her knowledge of the languages of the countries through which she had to pass was imperfect, and she was alone and unprotected. Yet her courage never failed her. The thought of Felix and the vision of a life of freedom sustained her through every hardship. After many weeks of weary travel, guided by Providence and the kindness of a few strangers, she at last arrived at the humble dwelling which I, too, had come to regard as a sanctuary. Her sudden appearance, as I had witnessed, was the event which had transformed the sorrow of the cottage into a newfound and tremulous joy.

This, then, was the story of my protectors. This long and sorrowful tale of human virtue and human treachery explained the poverty of the De Laceys and the sadness I had first observed in them; it also accounted for the radiant happiness that now illuminated their features since the arrival of the lovely stranger. My heart swelled with a strange tumult of emotions as I absorbed these revelations. I felt a profound admiration for the noble, self sacrificing Felix; a tender pity for the gentle Agatha and the venerable blind patriarch; and a love bordering on worship for the courageous and beautiful Safie. At the same time, a feeling of burning indignation towards the perfidious Turk and the unjust French tribunal filled my breast.

These narratives did more than simply satisfy my curiosity; they served as a further, more intimate lesson in the complexities of the human heart. I saw that for every act of vice and cruelty, there could exist an act of sublime virtue and generosity. The conduct of Felix, in particular, appeared to me as the very pinnacle of godlike benevolence. He had sacrificed his fortune, his country, and his personal safety for the sake of a principle, for a stranger whose only claim on him was his unjust suffering. This was the nobility which Volney's book had described, and to witness its living embodiment in my protector filled me with a reverence that words cannot express.

Yet, this very knowledge, this deeper insight into the capacity of man for goodness, only served to sharpen the sting of my own exclusion. I loved the cottagers with a devotion that consumed my entire being. In my solitude, I wept with them in their sorrows and thrilled with them in their joys. I saw in their interactions a portrait of the social affections that I now understood to be the chief source of human happiness. The tender care of Agatha for her father, the passionate love between Felix and Safie, the bonds of shared history and mutual support that united them all; these were the treasures for which I yearned, the paradise from which I was irrevocably barred.

My admiration for their virtues and my love for their persons grew to such a pitch that the desire to reveal myself, to cast myself at their feet and plead for their compassion, became an almost unbearable torment. I imagined myself explaining my strange existence, my utter loneliness, my harmless disposition. Surely, I thought, beings so kind and compassionate would not turn away a wretch whose only crime was his hideousness? Surely, the same heart that had bled for the oppressed Turk would feel some pity for a creature more solitary and miserable than any on earth? I would tell them of my lonely vigils, of the wood I secretly gathered for their fire, of the silent blessings I called down upon them from my hiding place. I would appeal not to their senses, but to their celebrated virtue.

The presence of the blind father seemed to offer the most promising avenue for my introduction. His eyes could not be shocked by my deformity. He would hear only the accents of my voice, a voice I had painstakingly modulated to imitate the gentle tones of Felix and Agatha. I could speak to him of my admiration, my reverence, and my desperate need for fellowship. He, in turn, might then intercede for me with his children. He could prepare them for my appearance and persuade them to look past the monstrous exterior to the sentient, feeling heart within.

This plan took root in my mind and grew with every passing day. It became the focus of all my thoughts, the one faint star of hope in the vast darkness of my despair. I resolved to wait for an opportunity when the old man should be alone. I would rehearse my speech, a plea for acceptance that I composed and recomposed a thousand times in the silence of my hovel. It would be a speech filled with the philosophical sentiments I had learned from Volney and the passionate feeling that was all my own. I would present myself not as a monster, but as a sensitive and rational being, worthy, if not of their love, then at least of their tolerance and compassion.

The approach of winter hastened my resolve. The leaves fell from the trees, stripping away my natural concealment and heralding the arrival of the snows that would confine my protectors indoors and render my nocturnal foraging more difficult. Time, I felt, was running out. My period of secret education was drawing to a close, and the hour of my great trial was at hand. I knew that the outcome of this single encounter would determine the entire course of my future existence. If I were accepted, I might find a place, however humble, in the society of sentient beings. If I were rejected, if even these, the most virtuous of mankind, should cast me out, then my heart would be hardened forever. I would turn from a supplicant into an enemy, and my future path would be one not of love and fellowship, but of hatred, revenge, and universal war. The fate of my soul, and perhaps the fate of others, rested upon the words of a blind old man in a lonely cottage. And so, with a heart trembling with a mixture of terror and hope, I began to watch and to wait for the moment that would decide all.

The very air was a knife, and the silence was broken only by the howl of the wind or the distant crack of a tree limb surrendering to the weight of the ice. This was my world, the one to which I had been consigned by my creator’s disgust.

I was traversing a dense and ancient wood, the pines heavy with snow, when I heard a cry, not of a beast, but of a human child. My first impulse was to flee, to retreat into the shadows where I belonged. But the sound was one of distress, and it pierced through my layers of bitterness to that part of me which had wept with Safie and yearned for the love of the cottagers. A young girl, hardly more than a child, had wandered from a nearby path and had fallen into a swift and turbulent stream, a dark gash in the white landscape where the current was too strong to freeze. She was struggling against the icy water, her cries growing weaker.
